## Ecological question

Can regional interaction structure help explain the nestedness and
modularity of six observed local plant–frugivore networks in Ecuador?
The records come from the [archived case
study](https://zenodo.org/records/5537283). The included data contain
observed interactions at six sites. We combine all recorded species
pairs into one regional network, also called a metaweb, and fit one
stochastic block model (SBM) to it. The SBM groups species by their
interaction patterns and estimates an interaction probability for each
pair of groups.

This supplement includes the records, the fitted regional model, and
results from 49 simulated networks for each scenario at each site. The
document loads the fitted model and simulation results when it renders;
the fitting and simulation code is shown for readers but is not run.
Only one small local network is reconstructed to illustrate MetaWeave.
The sites span 1,000, 2,000 and 3,000 m elevation, with two networks at
each level. Elevation orders the comparison; it is not an input to the
regional SBM. The question is whether its interaction probabilities and
the species present locally lead to different structural predictions
along this gradient.

We compare three ensembles at each site. Every simulated network has the
observed number of distinct links.

| Ensemble | Species | Link allocation |
|----|----|----|
| A: neutral | Observed local species | Equal chance among possible pairs |
| B: regional SBM | Observed local species | Weighted by regional SBM probabilities |
| C: changed composition | Random species from the regional pools, matched to local plant and frugivore richness | Weighted by the same regional SBM |

**B − A** changes the interaction rule while holding composition fixed.
**B − C** changes composition while holding the regional interaction
rule fixed. These are differences in network metrics, not z scores.
Random regional species are sampled with equal probability, an explicit
simplifying assumption about arrival and establishment.

## Load the regional model and reconstruct a site

We fit one SBM to the interactions pooled across all six sites. The
model assigns each plant and frugivore to a group and estimates a
probability of interaction for each combination of plant and frugivore
groups. These assignments and probabilities are included with the
supplement and form the regional input to MetaWeave. We use this same
model at every site.

In the first chunk, `block_model()` turns those saved assignments and
probabilities into one regional interaction rule. `new_assemblage()`
lists the plants and frugivores recorded at a site, and
`infer_network()` applies the rule to that assemblage. The returned
matrix contains one interaction probability for each locally possible
species pair.

```{r}
# Apply the pooled regional SBM to a locally recorded assemblage.
library(metaweave)
library(tidyverse)

source_data <- new.env()
load("data/ecuador/dataSet1.RData", envir = source_data)
records <- source_data$dataSet1$N
records <- records |>
  filter(frequency > 0) |>
  mutate(across(c(site, plantCode, animalCode), as.character))

regional <- readRDS("data/ecuador/pooled_sbm_fit.rds")
regional_rule <- block_model(
  regional$row_lookup, regional$column_lookup, regional$theta,
  "plants", "animals"
)

sites <- sort(unique(records$site))
first_site <- records |> filter(site == sites[1])
local_plants <- sort(unique(first_site$plantCode))
local_animals <- sort(unique(first_site$animalCode))
community <- new_assemblage(
  list(plants = local_plants, animals = local_animals), cell_id = 1L
)
local_probabilities <- infer_network(community, regional_rule)$matrix
tibble(site = sites[1], plants = nrow(local_probabilities),
       frugivores = ncol(local_probabilities),
       expected_links = round(sum(local_probabilities), 1)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "An example local network inferred from the regional SBM.")
```

Each entry of `local_probabilities` is the regional model's probability
for a pair whose species occur at this site. MetaWeave supplies this
local matrix. The next step uses its values as weights in a
fixed-link-count simulation; they are not independent Bernoulli draws.

### How the regional fit was obtained

To fit the regional model, we first combine the records from all six
sites into a single binary network. Its entries represent observed
species pairs: a pair is marked present if recorded at least once. The
following displayed code shows the essential fitting and translation
steps. It is not rerun in this document; `cassandRa` is required only
when fitting a new regional model.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
# Make one binary metaweb from all sites, ignoring repeat frequency.
plant_pool <- sort(unique(records$plantCode))
animal_pool <- sort(unique(records$animalCode))
metaweb <- matrix(0L, length(plant_pool), length(animal_pool),
                  dimnames = list(plant_pool, animal_pool))
metaweb[cbind(match(records$plantCode, plant_pool),
              match(records$animalCode, animal_pool))] <- 1L

# Fit once regionally; do not refit the model at individual sites.
set.seed(5537283)
candidate_fits <- cassandRa::FitSBM(
  list = cassandRa::CreateListObject(metaweb), n_SBM = 10, G = NULL
)
best <- candidate_fits$SBM1
theta <- best$Omega_rs
rownames(theta) <- paste0("plant_block_", seq_len(nrow(theta)))
colnames(theta) <- paste0("animal_block_", seq_len(ncol(theta)))
row_lookup <- tibble(species = plant_pool,
                     guild = rownames(theta)[as.integer(best$SB_H)])
column_lookup <- tibble(species = animal_pool,
                        guild = colnames(theta)[as.integer(best$SB_W)])
```

The regional network contains 102 plants, 127 frugivores and 536
recorded species pairs. The selected SBM has ten plant groups and ten
frugivore groups. The following table shows the estimated probabilities
between those groups, which `block_model()` uses to build local
predictions.

```{r}
# Display the regional network size and fitted interaction probabilities.
tibble(plants = nrow(regional$metaweb),
       frugivores = ncol(regional$metaweb),
       regional_links = sum(regional$metaweb),
       plant_blocks = nrow(regional$theta),
       frugivore_blocks = ncol(regional$theta)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Measure", values_to = "Value") |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Regional network and fitted block model.")
theta_table <- regional$theta
colnames(theta_table) <- paste0("F", seq_len(ncol(theta_table)))
rownames(theta_table) <- paste0("P", seq_len(nrow(theta_table)))
as_tibble(theta_table, rownames = "Plant group") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "Interaction probabilities for plant (P) and frugivore (F) groups.")
```

## Generate the comparison

The following code constructs the three sets of simulated networks. For
each site, it starts with the recorded species and links, then draws
networks under each of the three rules described above. The regional
model is fitted once to the pooled network; it is not refitted for each
draw.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Generate the three ensembles using the pooled regional model.
  library(vegan)
  library(bipartite)

  local_matrix <- function(x) {
    plants <- sort(unique(x$plantCode))
    animals <- sort(unique(x$animalCode))
    m <- matrix(0L, length(plants), length(animals),
                dimnames = list(plants, animals))
    m[cbind(match(x$plantCode, plants),
            match(x$animalCode, animals))] <- 1L
    m
  }
  
  probabilities <- function(plants, animals, id) {
    assemblage <- new_assemblage(
      list(plants = plants, animals = animals), cell_id = id
    )
    infer_network(assemblage, regional_rule)$matrix
  }
  
  
  fixed_links <- function(p, n, weighted) {
    positions <- sample.int(length(p), n, replace = FALSE,
                            prob = if (weighted) as.vector(p) else NULL)
    m <- matrix(0L, nrow(p), ncol(p))
    m[positions] <- 1L
    m
  }
  
  
  network_metrics <- function(m) {
    c(nodf = as.numeric(vegan::nestednodf(m)$statistic[["NODF"]]),
      modularity = as.numeric(bipartite::computeModules(m)@likelihood))
  }
  
```

Within each draw, `new_assemblage()` supplies either the observed
species or a richness-matched selection from the regional pool to
`infer_network()`. MetaWeave reconstructs the local probability matrix
under the *same* regional `block_model()` each time. The subsequent link
sampling and NODF and modularity calculations use base R, `vegan` and
`bipartite`; they follow MetaWeave's prediction. The document shows the
code and loads its saved output for the tables and figure.

```{r}
#| eval: false
  repetitions <- 49L
  set.seed(5537283)
  plant_pool <- sort(unique(records$plantCode))
  animal_pool <- sort(unique(records$animalCode))
  scenarios <- c("A_observed_neutral", "B_observed_sbm", "C_random_sbm")
  draws <- array(NA_real_, c(length(sites), repetitions, 3L, 2L),
                 dimnames = list(sites, NULL, scenarios,
                                 c("nodf", "modularity")))
  observed <- matrix(NA_real_, length(sites), 2L,
                     dimnames = list(sites, c("nodf", "modularity")))
  site_info <- data.frame(site = sites, elevation = NA_real_,
                          plants = NA_integer_, animals = NA_integer_,
                          links = NA_integer_)

  for (i in seq_along(sites)) {
    x <- records[records$site == sites[i], ]
    m <- local_matrix(x)
    n_links <- sum(m)
    site_info$elevation[i] <- unique(x$elevation)
    site_info$plants[i] <- nrow(m)
    site_info$animals[i] <- ncol(m)
    site_info$links[i] <- n_links
    observed[i, ] <- network_metrics(m)
    p_local <- probabilities(rownames(m), colnames(m), i)

    for (r in seq_len(repetitions)) {
      random_plants <- sort(sample(plant_pool, nrow(m)))
      random_animals <- sort(sample(animal_pool, ncol(m)))
      p_random <- probabilities(random_plants, random_animals, i)
      draws[i, r, "A_observed_neutral", ] <-
        network_metrics(fixed_links(p_local, n_links, FALSE))
      draws[i, r, "B_observed_sbm", ] <-
        network_metrics(fixed_links(p_local, n_links, TRUE))
      draws[i, r, "C_random_sbm", ] <-
        network_metrics(fixed_links(p_random, n_links, TRUE))
    }
  }
  analysis <- list(site_info = site_info, observed = observed,
                   draws = draws, reps = repetitions, seed = 5537283L)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
analysis <- readRDS("data/ecuador/assembly_mvp.rds")
```

### Sites along the gradient

The number of plants, frugivores and distinct links varies among sites.
Every ensemble retains its site's plant richness, frugivore richness and
link count, so the contrasts below do not arise simply from drawing
networks of different sizes.

The following table lists the elevation, recorded species richness and
number of distinct links at each site. These describe the observed
networks used to set the size of each simulation.

```{r}
# Describe the observed assemblages in elevation order.
site_table <- analysis$site_info |>
  as_tibble() |>
  arrange(elevation, site) |>
  select(site, elevation, plants, frugivores = animals, links)
site_table |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Site", "Elevation (m)", "Plants", "Frugivores", "Links"),
               caption = "Observed networks along the elevation gradient.")
```

## Read the contrasts

Nestedness (binary NODF) is higher when specialists' links tend to be
subsets of generalists' links. Modularity is higher when interactions
are more concentrated within groups. For each site we compare B with A
and C draw by draw, then show the mean difference and its central 95%
simulation interval. A circle in the figure represents **B − A**, the
effect of using regional interaction weights for the observed species; a
triangle represents **B − C**, the effect of keeping the observed
species instead of a richness-matched regional draw. Neither symbol is
an observed network metric.

The contrast chunk subtracts metrics calculated after sampling links
from MetaWeave's local probability matrices. It pairs draws within a
site and reports the mean and central interval of each metric
difference. The subtraction is in NODF or modularity units, not a
standardized score.

```{r}
# Calculate interaction-rule and composition contrasts within each site.
contrast <- function(metric, reference) {
  b <- analysis$draws[, , "B_observed_sbm", metric]
  other <- analysis$draws[, , reference, metric]
  difference <- b - other
  tibble(
    site = dimnames(analysis$draws)[[1]],
    metric = metric,
    contrast = paste("B -", substr(reference, 1, 1)),
    mean = rowMeans(difference),
    lower = apply(difference, 1, quantile, 0.025),
    upper = apply(difference, 1, quantile, 0.975)
  )
}

comparison <- bind_rows(
  contrast("nodf", "A_observed_neutral"),
  contrast("nodf", "C_random_sbm"),
  contrast("modularity", "A_observed_neutral"),
  contrast("modularity", "C_random_sbm")
  ) |>
  left_join(as_tibble(analysis$site_info) |>
              select(site, elevation), by = "site")
comparison |>
  arrange(elevation, site, metric, contrast) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "Mean contrasts and central 95% simulation intervals.")
```

The contrasts describe differences among simulated ensembles. The
observed networks provide another reference: for example, a site may be
more nested than all three ensemble means even when B − A is positive.
The following table keeps observed structure and the three simulated
means side by side. These means summarize 49 realizations, not 49 field
networks.

Here A, B and C summarize networks sampled after MetaWeave's
`infer_network()` step. The `observed` column comes from field records;
MetaWeave does not estimate that column.

```{r}
# Place observed metrics beside each ensemble's mean prediction.
ensemble_table <- map_dfr(c("nodf", "modularity"), function(metric) {
  tibble(
    site = analysis$site_info$site,
    elevation_m = analysis$site_info$elevation,
    metric = metric,
    observed = analysis$observed[, metric],
    A_neutral = rowMeans(analysis$draws[, , "A_observed_neutral", metric]),
    B_regional_SBM = rowMeans(analysis$draws[, , "B_observed_sbm", metric]),
    C_changed_species = rowMeans(analysis$draws[, , "C_random_sbm", metric])
  )
})
ensemble_table |>
  mutate(across(c(observed, A_neutral, B_regional_SBM,
                  C_changed_species), ~ round(.x, 2))) |>
  arrange(elevation_m, site, metric) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2,
               col.names = c("Site", "Elevation (m)", "Metric", "Observed", "A", "B", "C"),
               caption = "Observed network metrics and ensemble means.")
```

The figure plots the contrasts derived above, ordering the sites by the
elevation supplied with their observed records. It visualizes the
consequences of applying MetaWeave's regional rule to different local
assemblages and link-allocation scenarios; elevation itself is not a
predictor in `block_model()` or `infer_network()`.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Network assembly contrasts along the Ecuador elevation gradient. Sites are ordered from 1,000 to 3,000 m, with two sites per elevation. Circles show B − A (regional interaction rule); triangles show B − C (species composition). Points are means and vertical bars are central 95% intervals across 49 paired draws. The dashed line is zero difference."
# Keep site labels and both contrasts aligned along the elevation gradient.
site_labels <- site_table |>
  mutate(label = paste0(site, "\n", elevation, " m"))
plot_data <- comparison |>
  left_join(site_labels |> select(site, label), by = "site") |>
  mutate(label = factor(label, levels = site_labels$label),
         metric = recode(metric, nodf = "Nestedness (NODF)",
                         modularity = "Modularity"),
         contrast = recode(contrast, `B - A` = "Interaction rule: B − A",
                           `B - C` = "Composition: B − C"))

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = label, y = mean, colour = contrast,
                      shape = contrast, group = contrast)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.12,
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.45)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, position = position_dodge(width = 0.45)) +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_y", nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Interaction rule: B − A" = "#B2472F",
                                 "Composition: B − C" = "#246B91")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Interaction rule: B − A" = 16,
                                "Composition: B − C" = 17)) +
  labs(x = "Site and elevation along the gradient",
       y = "Difference in network metric", colour = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "bottom")
```

At the two 1,000-m sites, regional interaction weighting increased
nestedness by about 13 and 16 NODF units relative to uniform allocation,
and reduced modularity by about 0.05. The nestedness difference was
smaller at 2,000 m and its interval crossed zero at both 3,000-m sites.
The B − C nestedness intervals crossed zero at all six sites. This is a
pattern across these six networks, not a fitted elevation effect or a
test of a general altitudinal trend.

An interval crossing zero means these 49 simulations do not clearly
separate the two scenarios for that metric and site. The intervals
describe variation among simulated networks, not uncertainty across
Ecuadorian sites. The observed network is a separate reference; the
contrasts isolate modeling choices rather than proving that any process
caused its structure. The regional-pool randomization does not model
unequal dispersal, habitat filtering, or species' abundance.
